title: Ragnarök: The End Everyone Sees Coming
subtitle: Even the gods die — and the world after it begins again

learningObjectives.text: Why is Ragnarök different from a surprise ending?

prose.author: Snorri Sturluson
prose.locator: Gylfaginning 58, the renewed world; local text normalized characters 159549-159741
prose.excerpt: 58. Then said Ganglere: Do any gods live then? Is there any earth or heaven? Har answered: The earth rises again from the sea, and is green and fair. The fields unsown produce their harvests.
prose.note: Verbatim Rasmus B. Anderson translation excerpt; whitespace normalized.

poem.author: Anonymous Old Norse poets
poem.locator: Völuspá, stanzas 59-61; local text normalized characters 45061-45558
poem.excerpt: 59. Now do I see | the earth anew Rise all green | from the waves again; The cataracts fall, | and the eagle flies, And fish he catches | beneath the cliffs. 60. The gods in Ithavoll | meet together, Of the terrible girdler | of earth they talk, And the mighty past | they call to mind, And the ancient runes | of the Ruler of Gods. 61. In wondrous beauty | once again Shall the golden tables | stand mid the grass, Which the gods had owned | in the days of old, . . . . . . . . | . . . . . . . .
poem.note: Verbatim Henry Adams Bellows translation excerpt; whitespace normalized.

narrativeBlocks.title: The doom in the calendar
narrativeBlocks.body: Norse myth is unusual: the gods KNOW how it ends. Prophecies of Ragnarök — the world's final battle — run through the whole tradition, and the gods spend their time preparing, not denying.

narrativeBlocks.title: Fimbulwinter and the wolves
narrativeBlocks.body: The end comes on schedule: three winters without summer, the sun and moon devoured by the wolves that chase them, the bonds breaking. Loki slips free; the giants sail for the last war.

narrativeBlocks.title: The gods fall in order
narrativeBlocks.body: Odin is swallowed by the wolf Fenrir. Thor kills the world-serpent and dies nine steps later of its poison. Heimdall and Loki kill each other. Tyr falls to the hellhound. The destruction is total and mutual.

narrativeBlocks.title: And then the world again
narrativeBlocks.body: The earth sinks into the sea — then rises green. A new sun shines; the sons of the gods gather in a cleansed field; a man and woman hidden in the world-tree's trunk wake to seed humanity. Ragnarök is an ending that is also a beginning.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why this myth matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Most traditions end at paradise or punishment. The Norse ending is stranger: everything dies, and something better quietly sprouts. A people who built a theology around inevitable doom made their hope conditional but real.

quiz.prompt: What makes Ragnarök different from a surprise apocalypse?

choices.text: The gods know it's coming — prophecy runs through the whole tradition, and they prepare for a doom they can't prevent
It is a punishment the gods choose

quiz.explanation: The Norse cosmology builds the ending in from the start — knowledge doesn't prevent it.

choices.text: The earth rises green again — a new sun, the gods' surviving sons, and a hidden human pair repopulate the world
The gods return to Asgard unchanged

quiz.explanation: The myth's ending is renewal, not eternal darkness — the world after the doom.
